section_1.title: Introduction: The 'Broken' Pencil Mystery
section_1.content: Hook the audience with a visual demonstration of a pencil appearing broken when placed in a glass of water. Introduce the concept that light doesn't always travel in straight lines.
section_1.example: A pencil submerged in a glass of water appears offset at the surface; we explain this as light 'bending' when crossing media boundaries.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Speed of Light and Optical Density
section_2.content: Establish that light travels fastest in a vacuum and slows down when moving through denser materials (like water or glass). Define 'Refractive Index' (n) as the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed in the medium.
section_2.example: Visualize light as a 'marching line of soldiers' moving from a smooth pavement (air) into thick mud (water), causing them to slow down and change direction.

section_3.title: Core Principle: Snell's Law
section_3.content: Present Snell's Law (n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2)). Use a graphical split-screen: show the incident ray, the normal line, and the refracted ray. Animate the angles changing as the refractive index changes.
section_3.example: A laser beam hitting a glass block at an angle: display the calculated math on one side of the screen while the animation shows the ray bending toward the 'normal' line.

section_4.title: Nature's Adaptation: The Archerfish
section_4.content: Apply the theory to the Archerfish, which spits water at insects above the surface. Explain that the fish must compensate for the refraction of light to accurately aim at its prey.
section_4.example: An animation showing the Archerfish looking at an insect: the fish sees the 'apparent' position (refracted image) and aims slightly below where the prey appears to be.

section_5.title: Summary and Conclusion
section_5.content: Recap: Light slows down in denser media, causing it to bend toward the normal. This governs everything from the human eye's lens to fiber-optic cables in global communications.
section_5.example: A fast-paced montage: a lens focusing light onto a retina, a diamond sparkling due to internal refraction, and an fiber-optic pulse carrying high-speed internet.
